articles.title: Nvidia stock drops 6%, extending decline on report alleged Chinese spy linked to Nvidia CEO aided $7.5 billion in China chip shipments
articles.summary: Nvidia sank on Tuesday, while the rest of the chip sector held up.
articles.body:
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock extended its decline Tuesday, falling as much as 6% after dropping 4% in the prior session. The stock came under pressure amid a broader market sell-off and growing concerns about increased scrutiny of the chipmaker following CEO Jensen Huang's admission to an affair believed to involve a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Scrutiny centers on Alice Huang, whom the US government reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, and her ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dating back to at least 2023.

The Information reported that their rapport could have helped facilitate the shipment of at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Chinese companies, according to two people who know her and corporate records.

On Monday, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Congress needs more answers about the matter, adding that there are "real ⁠concerns that need to be addressed with respect to the ​Nvidia situation."

President Trump, meanwhile, told reporters that the FBI was looking into Huang's relationship, while still expressing support for the Nvidia CEO.

"We'll look into it," said Trump. "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape."

The broader semiconductor sector wavered on Tuesday amid a broader market sell-off after a hotter-than-expected October inflation reading, which strengthened expectations for a rate hike next month.

Rrival AMD ( AMD ) stock rose 4% before giving up gains. Broadcom ( AVGO ) shares gained more than 1%, while Intel ( INTC ) stock was little changed.

Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company ( TSM ), which manufactures Nvidia chips, wavered, while semiconductor equipment maker ASML ( ASML ) slipped into red territory.

Storage maker Sandisk ( SNDK ) and memory chipmakers Micron Technology ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) declined.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Real Risk Isn’t Jensen Huang’s Scandal. It’s The Family
articles.summary: Jensen Huang’s crisis is being read as a scandal. The bigger risk is the one family businesses know: a founder, a co-owner spouse and heirs, with no plan.
articles.body:
On November 8, Jensen Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife, Lori, and apologizing to his family and his staff. The same day, Nvidia's board said a committee of independent directors, working with outside counsel, would review reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised, and Nvidia says Huang will continue to lead the company without interruption.

Since then, the story has been told in two ways: as an espionage thriller, and as a guessing game about what Lori Huang might walk away with . Both miss what anyone who has advised a family firm will recognize immediately. This is a family business crisis, unfolding inside a company most people would never call a family business.

The family firm hiding inside a public company

Family business governance starts with a simple model. Renato Tagiuri and John Davis's three circles describe family, ownership and business as overlapping systems, and most governance failures happen where those circles meet. Map Nvidia onto it and the picture is striking.

The business circle: Jensen Huang, co-founder and CEO since 1993.

When the family and business intersects: Madison Huang joined Nvidia in 2020 and is now a senior director of product and technical marketing for its physical AI platform. Spencer Huang joined in 2022 and is a product line manager in robotics. Both work in areas the company sees as future growth engines, and their pay is disclosed in Nvidia's proxy statement.

Where family meets ownership: Nvidia's 2026 proxy lists Lori Huang as co-trustee, with her husband, of three family trusts that together held about 669 million Nvidia shares as of March 2026, including 528.5 million in the couple's living trust. She also sits on the board of the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, whose assets reached $9.2 billion in 2024, according to its tax filings.

Nvidia's board is built to govern the business circle. Nobody governs the space where family meets ownership. I call that the Invisible Circle . In a family firm, it would have a name, a forum and a set of rules. At Nvidia, it had none, until November 8 turned it into a market event.

Jensen Huang at the centre of the business

There is a second family business pattern at work here: the founder as the key person. Huang has run Nvidia since he co-founded it in 1993, which makes him one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in technology. He runs an unusually flat organization, with around 60 senior leaders reporting directly to him, and he has said he holds no one-on-one meetings with them. His keynotes set the market's expectations for the whole AI industry, and his leather jacket has become shorthand for the company itself.

articles.title: American paychecks are losing to inflation again — here are the most painful categories
articles.summary: Gas is getting cheaper, but airfares, restaurant meals, and power bills are rising faster than pay.
articles.body:
The gas pump is about the only place Americans are getting relief from inflation. Plane tickets, restaurant meals, and electric bills have all risen faster than the average worker's pay over the past two years.

Pump prices have fallen for six straight weeks . Even so, a gallon of gas still costs about 37% more than it did a year ago.

That's one of the few yearly numbers the government could publish Tuesday. The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not collect October 2025 prices during last year's shutdown, so the usual annual inflation rate is missing.

So we estimated it. According to Yahoo Finance's calculations, consumer prices rose about 4% in the year through October, up from 3.7% in September.

Paychecks didn't keep up. Average hourly pay rose about 3%, which leaves pay down nearly 1% after inflation. That's the seventh straight month workers have lost ground, matching May as the worst stretch of the run.

And prices are speeding up. They rose 0.4% in October, while "core" prices , which leave out food and energy, rose 0.3%. Both came in hotter than Wall Street expected.

Over the past three months, core prices climbed at a nearly 4% annual pace, noted Kevin Gordon, head of macro research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research. That's the fastest since April 2024, per Yahoo Finance's calculations.

"For households, the reduced purchasing power from inflation hits twice as hard when your wages aren't keeping up," Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360, said in emailed comments.

Since October 2024, average hourly pay has increased by about 7%. Here's what outran it.

Airfares jumped more than 20%. Car repairs rose by about 13%, hospital services by about 12%, and electricity by nearly 10%. A meal at a sit-down restaurant costs about 9% more.

Groceries are the exception, up only about 5%.

Take the average of four costs most households can't skip — the "utility, gasoline, grocery, and electricity components" of the index — and they're up 12% from a year ago, Gordon wrote on X .

The war in the Middle East is a major reason, according to RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas. He pointed to "the passing through of higher energy prices — think diesel prices — to transportation services and food at home." Diesel , the fuel that powers nearly everything else, is still near its record high.

That leaves the Federal Reserve on track to raise interest rates, which would push up borrowing costs on credit cards, car loans, and other debt. Fed governor Chris Waller said Tuesday he's leaning toward a December hike and would consider a half point , double the usual move, if inflation runs hot. Traders on Polymarket see a better-than-90% chance of a hike when the Fed meets on Dec. 8-9.

articles.title: Anthropic launches Meetings, Whiteboards, Sheets, Data ahead of IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic launched a handful of new enterprise tools Tuesday as it prepares for its initial public offering.
articles.body:
Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) is expanding further into the enterprise software space with the debut of five new offerings that bring its Claude platform to more work-based tools.

On Tuesday, the company debuted Claude Meetings, Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, Claude Data, and interactive connectors that bring Claude into full versions of third-party software.

Microsoft stock fell more than 2% on the news.

The announcements come as Anthropic kicks off its roadshow ahead of its initial public offering, expected on either Nov. 19 or Nov. 20 . The company could be valued at up to $1.4 trillion when it hits the market.

Anthropic said Claude Meetings feature allows Claude to join video calls, follow conversations, answer questions in the meeting chat, and pull information from connected apps.

Claude Whiteboards begins putting together a whiteboard with timelines and responsibilities as teams talk through planning strategies, and Claude Sheets can build a spreadsheet based on information a colleague is working on.

Claude Data can grab data from different platforms and provide answers in the form of videos, written summaries, and dashboards.

Anthropic's enterprise offerings have previously set off alarm bells among software-as-a-service developers and investors, sending shares of companies including Salesforce ( CRM ), ServiceNow ( NOW ), and Intuit ( INTU ) plunging earlier this year.

The AI lab's enterprise efforts have also been a boon for its bottom line.

Revenue grew $1,206% to $33.2 billion through the first nine months of the year that ended Sept. 30.

For the first six months of the year through June 30, Anthropic's revenue was $16.3 billion. The company recorded sales of $4.6 billion in all of 2025.

Rival OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), which initially focused on the consumer market, is also gaining traction in the enterprise market. In August, CNBC reported that CFO Sarah Friar told investors that the company's enterprise revenue had eclipsed consumer revenue.

articles.title: Rising medical costs are piling on for seniors already squeezed by inflation
articles.summary: Medical care expenses — one of the biggest costs seniors face — are rising, according to the latest Consumer Price Index data.
articles.body:
Medical expenses — one of the biggest costs seniors face — are rising fast with little relief in sight.

While overall consumer prices were up 0.4% month over month , according to the latest figures, older Americans have been slammed by rising healthcare costs for months.

Medical care items were up 0.5% and medical services rose 0.3%. Hospital services rose 0.8% over the month, and doctors' services increased 0.4%. Prescription drugs rose 0.3% in October.

Dental services, which are not covered by Medicare, jumped 0.8% in October and 0.5% the previous month.

The biggest jump was the cost of medical equipment and supplies, which rose 1.4% in October on top of 0.4% in September and 1.0% in August. This includes adhesive strips, heating pads, wheelchairs, a chair for the shower, and compression socks among other items regularly used by older Americans.

"What makes these rising healthcare costs so alarming is that they're affecting virtually every aspect of seniors' medical needs, from doctor and dental visits to prescription drugs, hospital stays, medical equipment, and home healthcare," Shannon Benton, executive director of the Senior Citizens League, a nonprofit advocacy organization, told Yahoo Finance.

The costs for nursing homes and adult care increased by 0.3% in October. Home healthcare rose by 0.2%.

"These aren't luxuries; they're necessities that older Americans often have little choice but to pay for. Seniors can't simply stop taking medications, skip necessary treatments, or go without nursing home or home healthcare because prices have gone up," she said.

"Seniors can't budget their way out of getting sick or needing medication."

Then there's the cumulative impact. Seniors are already struggling with higher housing costs, groceries, utilities, and Medicare premiums . "Now they're being asked to absorb even more increases in essential healthcare expenses, often on fixed incomes that simply aren't keeping pace," she said.

Roughly 15% of the average retiree's annual expenses will be health-related, according to Fidelity.

On average, a 65-year-old who leaves the workforce this year may need $185,500 in savings to cover out-of-pocket healthcare expenses throughout retirement even when enrolled in traditional Medicare. (Don't forget, Medicare isn't free , and it doesn't pay for everything.)

That estimate also doesn't include long-term care expenses, over-the-counter medications, and most dental services.

An apartment in an assisted-living facility is averaging $87,000 this year, according to the National Investment Center for Seniors Housing & Care — and costs go up as residents age and need more care. Units for dementia patients have an average rate of $105,000.

articles.title: Chip stocks' slide nears $5 trillion as Nvidia hits most extreme selling level since 2019
articles.summary: Nvidia and memory stocks are dragging chips lower again after a hot inflation report, even as most S&P 500 stocks hold up.
articles.body:
It took five minutes for Tuesday's hot inflation report to knock stocks lower, and chip stocks struggled to hold an early rebound. Nvidia ( NVDA ) hasn't been sold this hard, this fast since 2019, but the typical S&P 500 stock is barely down.

The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) was down nearly 1% midday Tuesday, shedding about $500 billion in market value according to Yahoo Finance calculations, while the PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) fell more than 1%. The equal-weighted S&P 500 ( ^SPXEW ), which gives every company the same weight, was down only about 0.2%.

Nvidia fell about 6%, slicing through the $170 level chart watchers flagged, and is on track for its lowest close since March 30 as the scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang drags on. Its relative strength index , a gauge of how fast and how hard a stock has moved, sank to 23 out of a possible 100 — its most oversold reading since June 2019.

Memory makers Micron ( MU ) and SanDisk ( SNDK ) and chip designer Arm ( ARM ) fell roughly 3% to 5%. AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) held up after Monday's surge.

The longer view is starker. A Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks has lost about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, roughly a quarter of its worth. That's more than the roughly $3 trillion the entire S&P 500 has shed over the same stretch, even though the basket includes some companies outside the index.

Tuesday's trigger was a hotter-than-expected October Consumer Price Index . S&P 500 futures fell about 0.5% in the five minutes after the 8:30 a.m. ET release, on volume many times the morning's norm. Nasdaq-100 futures briefly erased their losses by 10 a.m., then slid again.

Bonds felt it too. The 5-year Treasury yield ( ^FVX ) was on track for its biggest one-day jump since April 2025, and the 10-year ( ^TNX ) climbed back above 5% as traders raised bets on a December rate hike .

BofA's Savita Subramanian sees the bigger risk in the S&P 500 itself.

"We're not particularly bullish on the index. I think the index itself is a bit risky," the head of US equity and quantitative strategy at BofA Securities told Yahoo Finance on Tuesday. "What's the most crowded equity ticker in the world? It's the S&P index."

The typical stock looks nothing like the index. The equal-weighted S&P 500 is up about 4% since Oct. 6 and closed at a record on Nov. 4.

Some see Nvidia's slide as a chance to buy. "I think if [CEO Jensen Huang] stays, then this is going to prove to be overdone. And you know this will be a strong buying opportunity," Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon said Monday on Yahoo Finance's "Deirdre Bosa Live."

articles.title: Nvidia hires former acting U.S. attorney to probe Jensen Huang affair
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board of directors has hired a former prosecutor to probe events surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman believed to be a spy for China.
articles.body: Nvidia’s board of directors announced Tuesday that it has hired a prominent former prosecutor and a top Wall Street law firm to probe the events surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman believed to be a spy for China. “The independent members of the NVIDIA Board have retained former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a thorough and independent investigation as was announced on Sunday,” the company said in a statement. The announcement followed revelations over the weekend that included Huang’s admission that had an extramarital affair. The woman with whom Huang had the affair is widely believed to be Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and business executive. U.S. intelligence agencies believe that Huang spied for the Chinese government, sources told NBC News. As of Tuesday, Jensen Huang remained in his post as Nvidia’s CEO, and a spokesperson for the company told NBC News over the weekend that he was focused on leading the trillion-dollar AI chip giant “without interruption.” President Donald Trump said Monday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was also probing the events. Trump said Huang “had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” adding, “I really believe him.” The recent developments have caused Nvidia shares to sell-off by more than 10% since trading opened on Monday morning. The move has erased almost $500 billion of value from the $4 trillion company in just two days. The sell-off was the latest blow in a weeks long decline for Nvidia stock already underway. After hitting its last record high on October 6, shares in the chip designer have plunged by 31%. That drop has erased more than $1.7 trillion in market value. Adding to the downward pressure on Nvidia shares Tuesday was new reporting from The New York Times that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had twice warned Trump about Huang’s entanglement with Chinese intelligence. “Trump was told aboard Air Force One in May en route to China that the United States had obtained sensitive intelligence showing that Nvidia’s chief executive was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy,” the Times reported. NBC News has not confirmed the report and has reached out to the State Department for comment. Rubio’s warning to Trump reportedly came shortly before Huang joined Trump aboard Air Force One during a pitstop in Alaska on its way to Beijing, where Trump was making a state visit. Huang had not been among the White House’s initial list of business leaders invited on the trip, according to reports at the time. But Trump denied this, writing on social media May 12 that Huang would be joining him on the state visit. “Jensen is currently on Air Force One,” Trump posted, mid-flight. On Monday, Trump was asked if he had been briefed about Huang before that trip. “I didn’t hear about it then,” Trump claimed. Pressed a second time about when he became aware of Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy, Trump said he would “have to check.” “They could have been mentioned,” he said. “Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” “He’s an amazing guy,” Trump said of Huang, “I hope there’s no problem.” “If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it,” the president continued, “but I hope there’s no problem.”

articles.title: Fed’s Waller opens door to half-point rate hike in December
articles.summary: Christopher Waller, a member of the Federal Reserve board of governors, said Tuesday he may support a half-point interest rate hike next month depending on what economic data indicates. During the Bank of England Watchers’ Conference, Waller said that “even if” inflation data for October is an improvement over September, he is “leaning toward” supporting…
articles.body:
Christopher Waller, a member of the Federal Reserve board of governors, said Tuesday he may support a half-point interest rate hike next month depending on what economic data indicates.

During the Bank of England Watchers’ Conference, Waller said that “even if” inflation data for October is an improvement over September, he is “leaning toward” supporting a quarter-point rate hike at the Federal Open Market Committee’s (FOMC) next meeting , set for Dec. 8-9.

But Waller noted that is his plan if economic trends play out as he anticipates. If consumer price index (CPI) data for October showed core prices rising by at least 0.3 percent, a “stronger policy move” may be in the cards, the Fed governor argued.

“In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting,” he said at King’s College London. “Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.”

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) released CPI data for October on Tuesday, reporting that prices rose by 0.4 percent from September to last month. Core prices, which do not account for energy and food costs, rose by 0.3 percent for the third straight month, the benchmark Waller referenced.

Energy and food prices, respectively, rose by 0.7 percent and 0.5 percent, while electricity prices experienced their largest monthly jump since April, rising by 0.9 percent, the BLS reported.

FOMC officials hiked interest rates by a quarter point in September, as they attempt to bring inflation down to their 2 percent target after five and a half years of elevated prices.

“Economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above the FOMC’s 2 percent goal,” Waller noted Tuesday.

Officials held rates steady at a rate of 3.75 percent to 4 percent in late October. Traders are pricing in a 90.5 percent chance of the FOMC raising rates by a quarter point next month and a 9.5 percent chance of a 50-basis-point increase, according to the CME FedWatch tool .

After Waller delivered his Tuesday remarks and the BLS reported the latest inflation data, bond yields in the U.S. spiked. The 10-year Treasury bond yield topped 5 percent for the first time in a week during intraday trading, and is up nearly 13 basis points from Monday’s closing bell.

The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond , meanwhile, nearly reached 5.38 percent during Tuesday trading, reaching its highest point since Oct. 29. The note is trading at about 5.35 percent as of the mid afternoon.

articles.title: Traders Who Rushed to Safety of Bonds Get Rattled in Reversal
articles.summary: A recent influx of bullish positioning across the US bond market just got smacked, as comments from a pair of Federal Reserve officials and fresh evidence of...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- A recent influx of bullish positioning across the US bond market just got smacked, as comments from a pair of Federal Reserve officials and fresh evidence of sticky inflation increased the odds of interest-rate hikes, sending Treasuries into a tailspin.

Tuesday's selloff rippled throughout the Treasury curve, with traders pricing in a more aggressive Fed tightening path after Governor Christopher Waller said he supported a rate increase and that he'd favor a half-point hike if inflation continued to accelerate. A hotter-than-expected consumer price report added fuel to the shift, as did further hawkish comments from Dallas Fed President Lori Logan.

The rout — which sent two-year US yields soaring by the most in 19 months and briefly pushed 10-year yields back over 5% — upended investors who lately had been flocking to Treasuries or turning less bearish in response to recent market jitters around the AI trade.

Over the last week, asset managers continued to establish long positions in futures across the curve, while covering bearish wagers in the long end, Bank of America Corp. strategists wrote in a Nov. 8 note.

Now, though, with traders increasingly pricing in "frontloading" of Fed tightening into the March meeting next year, the policy-sensitive two-year yield "still has room to get where we were at the end of September," when it peaked just shy of 5%, said Ed Al-Hussainy, portfolio manager at Columbia Threadneedle Investments. It ended Tuesday at 4.73%.

In the cash market, the divergent cross-currents have left some investors struggling for direction. JPMorgan Chase & Co.'s Treasury client survey released Tuesday reveals diminishing levels of conviction, with safe-haven tactical longs and longer-term short positions battling against each other. The poll showed both long and short positions dropping sharply, leaving neutrals at their most elevated in about 12 weeks.

Not all traders were wrong-footed by Tuesday's selloff. In the options market, flows over the past week have started to show signs that traders are unwinding safe-haven hedges. On Monday, a large seller of five-year January 107.00 calls appeared to unwind a bullish hedge set in late October, though at a loss of roughly $3 million.

articles.title: Exports to West Asia fall 7%, Jordan, Oman buck the trend
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India's exports to West Asia fell 7.2% during the first half of the current financial year, with Oman and Jordan bucking the trend.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India's exports to West Asia fell 7.2% during the first half of the current financial year, with Oman and Jordan bucking the trend. While Oman gained due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Jordan was a surprise, with exports from India doubling on account of a spike in buffalo meat, oil products and pharma exports.Among the top products exported from India to the Gulf nations, jewellery, oil products and mobile phones have seen a dip, while ships and boats and basmati rice are among the top gainers. Shipments of petrol and diesel to GCC and other West Asian countries are estimated to have fallen 27% to $3.5 billion, while gold and other jewellery to the Gulf trading bloc is down 8.6% to $3.2 billion, latest available data with the commerce department showed.While exports to Oman have jumped 45% to $3.2 billion during April-Sept, the value of goods shipped to Jordan soared 2.4 times to $1.2 billion. In case of Oman, the free trade agreement was implemented a few months ago, which has provided a boost to Indian exports, particularly products such as ships and boats, processed minerals, some chemicals, basmati rice and iron and steel. While some of the goods are for the Oman market, the country's port is also acting as the gateway to the UAE as the Strait of Hormuz was shut and traffic still remains disrupted.In case of Jordan, four product groups added $592.7 million, accounting for 85% of the total increase of Indian exports of close to $700 million during April-Sept, trade think tank GTRI said. Petrol and diesel nearly trebled from $110.3 million to $327.3 million. Rice, mostly basmati, shot up from $47.6 million to $253.5 million, while buffalo meat exports rose from $48.8 million to $192.4 million and medicine exports rose from $13.5 million to $39.7 million, it said.Trade body Fieo said with Jordan's rising fuel demand, India has strengthened its position by supplying approximately 9,000 barrels a day, although Saudi Arabia remains the dominant source. "Jordan may increasingly be serving a dual role for Indian exporters - as a growing destination market in its own right and as a potential gateway to other markets in West Asia and North Africa. articles.title: Premium upgrades drive appliances' festive sales
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India's festive appliance season exposed a divide in what shoppers were willing to pay for.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India's festive appliance season exposed a divide in what shoppers were willing to pay for. Bigger televisions and higher-capacity appliances found buyers, while demand for some of the cheapest TV sets faded as Diwali approached. Several brands reported faster growth in sales value than in units, helped by both higher prices and a shift towards costlier models. Air conditioners were an exception at some companies, with more units sold as well as higher takings."Our premium television portfolio witnessed significant momentum, recording 600% growth this festive season, while our air purifier category recorded over 300% YoY growth this festive season," a Xiaomi India spokesperson said. The company did not disclose the volumes behind either figure.Hisense India sold 25% more units from Navratri to Dhanteras than in the same festive period last year, while sales value rose 35%. CEO Pankaj Rana said its TV business grew about 35% and ACs about 20%, without specifying whether those figures referred to units or value.At Thomson, early Navratri offers drew shoppers who had put off purchases, but sales momentum later weakened at the budget end. Avneet Singh Marwah, CEO of Super Plastronics, the Indian licensee for Thomson, Kodak and Blaupunkt, said higher input and freight costs had made buyers of entry-level sets more cautious. "In contrast, the premium segment witnessed robust growth of over 20%," he said, citing strong demand for 55-inch and 65-inch TVs.Intex Technologies reported a roughly 45% rise in festive sales value, with volume growth trailing. TVs, ACs and washing machines led the gains, with small appliances and speakers also contributing. Director Keshav Bansal said higher input costs and currency movements prompted price increases, while larger screens and higher-capacity appliances lifted the average bill. "Consumers were willing to spend more when they saw a meaningful difference in what the product offered," he said. articles.title: Whitmer presses Trump administration on tariffs, grocery reimbursements
articles.summary: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) is pressing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other Trump administration officials to end new tariffs and issue grocery reimbursements for Michigan residents being hit with rising prices. “The unpredictable federal tariff policy has left Michiganders with the highest tariff burden in the nation,” Whitmer wrote in a letter to Bessent.…
articles.body:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) is pressing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other Trump administration officials to end new tariffs and issue grocery reimbursements for Michigan residents being hit with rising prices.

“The unpredictable federal tariff policy has left Michiganders with the highest tariff burden in the nation,” Whitmer wrote in a letter to Bessent. “Today, I am writing to ask the federal government to end the new tariffs on food levied in 2025 and 2026, and reimburse Michiganders for the costs they have incurred as a result of those tariffs.”

She cited a study done by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation that reported Michigan households held a tariff burden of $6,485 per household since January 2025 – the highest in the country.

Whitmer referenced another report from the Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development that noted tariffs contributed to a 3 percent increase in Michigan food prices last year.

The Wolverine State is among the top states estimated to be hit hard by President Trump’s ongoing trade war with Canada. Michigan is largely dependent on Canada for trade – importing more than $43.5 billion in goods per year from the country. The state also exports $21.2 billion worth of goods to Canada every year, including $726 million in engines and turbines, $559 million in crude petroleum, and $346 million in aircraft and parts.

Many of these goods are affected by current Canadian and U.S. tit-for-tat tariffs ranging from 25 to 50 percent.

Whitmer stated she believed declining trade with Canada was “signaling severe strain with our strongest trading partner.”

“These tariffs and sudden policy reversals have weakened Michigan’s competitiveness and disrupted long-standing trade relationships,” she continued.

“In my interactions with the federal government, including with President Trump, I have been fighting for a smarter, strategic trade policy, and I will keep at it,” Whitmer concluded. “But without tangible relief from the federal government, Michigan families will continue to bear the costs.”

It is unclear how much in reimbursements Whitmer is requesting.

Trump has signaled the Canadian trade war will end “ pretty soon ” but has not given a definitive timeline. He has also threatened to increase tariffs on Canadian automobiles and related parts on New Year’s Day.

The Treasury Department did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: Tech, heavy engineering lead profit growth in manufacturing
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: High-value segments, such as technology, heavy engineering and automotive segments, have led the profit growth in India's organised
articles.body: NEW DELHI: High-value segments, such as technology, heavy engineering and automotive segments, have led the profit growth in India's organised manufacturing sector in 2024-25, the latest annual survey of industries (ASI) data showed. Despite headwinds, these sectors ensured resilient overall value addition and broader wage distribution across the formal manufacturing sector.Among industries, computer and electronic products recorded a 46% jump in profits to Rs 41,100 crore, alongside a 20% expansion in the wage bill (Rs 33,800 crore). Fabricated metals manufacturing matched this momentum in profits, with a 46% profit jump to Rs 34,180 crore.The ASI data showed that net profit in the overall formal manufacturing sector rose 7.7% in 2024-25 to reach Rs 11.6 lakh crore, while the total wage bill - including salary, bonus and employers' contribution in the form of provident fund - expanded 12.3% to nearly Rs 9 lakh crore.The pharmaceutical industry saw a 24% jump in profits to Rs 1.2 lakh crore, while its wage bill increased 19% to Rs 69,300 crore. Labour intensive industries, which employ a vast majority of the formal manufacturing workforce such as textiles and wearing apparel, saw their profitability rise 34% (Rs 24,232 crore) and 30% (Rs 17,567 crore) respectively. Wage bill for these industries, however, grew moderately. Textiles saw a 10% rise to Rs 52,749 crore, while total wages in the wearing apparel rose 17% to Rs 40,888 crore.Core heavy industries and consumer segments also posted robust gains. Basic metals generated the highest absolute net profits among major groups at Rs 1.4 lakh crore (12.7% rise), while the wage bill crossed Rs 80,000 crore. articles.title: Cheaper Scotch raises stakes for desi whisky
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Cheaper Scotch is putting Indian whisky makers under pressure, even as lower import duties offer savings to companies that use it in their
articles.body: BENGALURU: Cheaper Scotch is putting Indian whisky makers under pressure, even as lower import duties offer savings to companies that use it in their blends. For small distillers that make their own spirits, an imported label can now cost substantially less than a locally made bottle.Huli's rice malt whisky was launched in Karnataka at Rs 2,650 for 750ml. By comparison, J&B Rare was priced at Rs 1,375 at Bengaluru retailer Tonique in October, according to TOI's earlier reporting. At these prices, J&B Rare cost Rs 1,275 less, or about half as much. Tonique said the price had fallen from Rs 2,835, attributing the reduction to local bottling."The smaller players will not be able to survive," said Huli Spirits founder Aruna Urs. Her Mysuru distillery makes spirits from locally sourced paddy and jaggery and does not import Scotch.Arun Kumar Parasa of Unistil Alcoblends said falling Scotch prices had adversely affected the Indian single malt industry. Lower duties on bulk Scotch imported by some small and medium distilleries would benefit them "very marginally", he said.The distinction is between making spirits locally and buying imported whisky for bottling or blending. Bulk Scotch arrives in large containers and can be bottled here or used as an ingredient in Indian whisky.A lower import bill can help these manufacturers, while cheaper finished bottles intensify competition for other producers.Jason Holway, senior consultant at drinks research firm IWSR, expects the price gap to narrow further. "Depending on the state, cheaper blended Scotches are expected to become more attractively priced than they used to be and may not be much more expensive than domestic premium brands using Scotch as an ingredient."India's trade agreement with Britain cut Scotch import duties from 150% to 75%. Customs officials subsequently questioned whether certain bulk shipments qualified for the lower duty. On Nov 2, commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal assured manufacturers that the duty benefits would be protected, with commerce and revenue officials to work on resolving the classification dispute.An industry executive, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Indian buyers were also negotiating better purchase prices from Scotland. The executive estimated that the duty reduction could lower retail prices by roughly 8-10%, depending on state taxes and companies' pricing decisions. Distribution difficulties and advertising restrictions remained longstanding hurdles for small manufacturers, the executive added.IWSR's figures also show the limits of India's shift towards expensive whisky. Its premium-and-above category, defined as Rs 2,899.01 or more per 750ml bottle, accounted for less than 1% of whisky consumed by volume in 2025, Holway said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bond yields surge most in 19 months as traders brace for Fed rate hikes
articles.summary: US Treasuries slumped, pushing yields sharply higher, after hotter-than-expected inflation data and comments from a key Federal Reserve official fueled bets that the central bank would need to deliver more aggressive interest rate hikes to cool inflation.
articles.body: US Treasuries slumped, pushing yields sharply higher, after hotter-than-expected inflation data and comments from a key Federal Reserve official fueled bets that the central bank would need to deliver more aggressive interest rate hikes to cool inflation. The two-year Treasury yield, which closely tracks expectations for Fed policy, surged 17 basis points on Tuesday. The two-year yield saw its biggest single-day jump since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s unveiling of tariffs rocked financial markets. The rocky day for bonds started after Fed Governor Chris Waller said during remarks in London that he would consider backing a jumbo rate hike of 50 basis points (a half point) at the US central bank’s December policy meeting if core inflation – a measure that strips out the volatile categories of food and energy – continues to come in at 0.3% or higher. “Then, a stronger policy move may be needed,” he said. “Hiking only 25 basis points [a quarter point] would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.” Waller said he wants to monitor how the AI buildout is impacting prices of high-tech goods, and if the rise in energy prices this year is continuing to add to inflationary pressures. Oil prices have dropped in recent days, but remain well-above their pre-Iran war levels. Consumer price data released Tuesday showed core inflation rose 0.3% from a month earlier, more than the 0.2% increase economists had expected. Yields surged higher after the data release. The key 10-year Treasury yield jumped 10 basis points to 4.98% and briefly rose above 5% during trading. The 10-year yield influences the cost of borrowing across the economy, most notably mortgage rates. An auction of 10-year notes on Tuesday saw soft demand, according to market strategist Peter Boockvar, adding to pressure on bonds. Meanwhile, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said in remarks in Houston on Tuesday that the Fed needs to deliver at least two additional quarter-point rate increases. “The exact pace of increases could depend on the near-term economic and financial environment,” Logan said. “It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the [Fed] has moved so far this fall.” Traders are now pricing in a 91% chance of a quarter-point rate hike and a 9% chance of a half-point rate hike in December, according to CME FedWatch. Just one week ago, traders were pricing in a 77% chance of a quarter-point hike and a 23% chance of the Fed holding rates steady. “October’s economic data profile and a hawkish shift in Fed-speak have prompted the market to reassess whether a faster pace of Fed policy tightening may be warranted,” Vail Hartman, US rates strategist at BMO Capital Markets, wrote in a note. Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander, said in a note that he remains convinced the Fed will hike rates by 25 basis points in December, adding that Waller’s consideration of 50 basis points likely doesn’t represent the consensus view among Fed officials. “Having said that, I would also note that if the inflation data do not show signs of improvement in the coming months, then my expectation of no further tightening in 2027 is in jeopardy,” Stanley wrote. Stocks closed slightly lower Tuesday. The S&P 500 was down 0.4% and the Nasdaq ticked down by 0.74%. Nvidia shares fell 5.47%, extending a recent bout of weakness over concerns about the board’s investigation into reports CEO Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Nvidia shares closed at their lowest level since March 30.

articles.title: Why this top Wall Street strategist isn't bullish on the S&P 500 for 2027
articles.summary: The S&P 500 could be a tough one to rally around in 2027.
articles.body:
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) could be a tough one to rally around in 2027.

"We're not particularly bullish on the index," Bank of America head of US equity and quantitative strategy Savita Subramanian said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I think the index itself is a bit risky because the other thing that I worry about is we've been in a 30-, 40-year period where we've seen S&P index inflows every year. We've never been in a market environment where the index has seen outflows. So I worry about that to some extent, because we're now at a point where investors are fairly saturated in equities across the board. You look at individuals, you look at asset owners and what's the most crowded equity ticker in the world … it's the S&P 500 index."

All things being considered, this year has been decent for investors — though at times it hasn't felt like it .

The year has been defined by whiplash as the US war on Iran sparked an aggressive oil price shock that pushed crude past $100 per barrel and reignited stubborn headline inflation.

To combat persistent price pressures — seen in today's October CPI reading , for example — Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh executed the first interest rate hike of the cycle in September, lifting the policy rate to 3.75% to 4%. Calls are now rising for the Fed to lift interest rates by 50 basis points at its final policy meeting in December.

Simultaneously, an unprecedented artificial intelligence boom drove tech valuations and hyperscaler capital expenditures into overdrive throughout the first half of the year. That exuberance turned into a sharp bust this fall, as slowing data center approvals, Election Day shifts, and soaring debt-financing costs triggered violent multiple compression and historic equity sell-offs across chipmakers and neoclouds.

The S&P 500 is up 9.5% year to date, outperforming the Dow Jones Industrial Average's ( ^DJI ) 8.5% advance and the 7.5% rise for the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ).

Subramanian warned, "So if you need to raise capital to meet your yield obligations or whatnot, I think that that's where things get a little bit interesting in terms of outflows. And that's where we see some risks to this thesis that the S&P 500 is just going to go up forever."

articles.body:
Lawmakers react to October inflation data

Lawmakers and incoming lawmakers noted Tuesday that the latest inflation data for October show the economy is still dealing with upward price pressures .

“It’s just another brick in the wall for people that can’t … make it,” Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine) told The Hill.

Prices rose by 0.4 percent from September to October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported Tuesday. Energy, food and shelter prices respectively spiked by 0.7 percent, 0.5 percent and 0.3 percent.

Electricity prices, meanwhile, increased by 0.9 percent from September. That marked the highest monthly jump for the utility since April, the BLS noted.

Rep. Rick Allen (R-Ga.) noted “we know what the drivers are” of persistent inflation, pointing out elevated oil prices.

The average price of gas dipped below $4 per gallon on Tuesday but remains roughly $1 higher than two days before the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war, according to AAA.

Allen, though, argued the Russia-Ukraine war is “affecting” oil prices “as much” as the Iran conflict, which is in its ninth month.

The Georgia Republican also said prices are in better shape than they were under the Biden administration. In January 2025, the month of President Trump’s second inauguration, annual inflation was 3 percent .

The BLS did not report annual inflation data for October, as last fall’s record-long government shutdown hindered the bureau’s ability to collect data on prices. But annual inflation in September was 3.7 percent .

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) faulted Trump for persistent inflation, noting Americans are facing high gas, grocery and housing costs.

“Last week, Americans across the country made clear that Donald Trump’s economic agenda is a failure,” Warren added in a statement, referencing Democrats’ midterm victories . “It’s time for Congress to act and deliver relief for families across this country.”

Jackson, who said he wants to join the Senate Banking and Finance committees , struck a similar tone.

The Maine Democrat, fresh off his victory over Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) said the latest inflation data is “one more reason” for lawmakers “to try and do some stuff to help people.”

articles.title: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar says China's lead in model pricing is 'one of the myths of 2026'
articles.summary: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar says Chinese AI model's aren't always the least expensive option.
articles.body:
OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) CFO Sarah Friar argued Tuesday that the company's lightweight Luna model is far less expensive than competing open-weight Chinese models, while still offering strong overall performance.

Open-weight models, or models that users can customize and run on their own hardware, are seen as a cost-saving measure for businesses that want to spend less on AI without having to cut back on using the technology. And China dominates the market.

OpenRouter , which tracks real-world usage of models accessed through its model-picking platform, shows seven of the top 10 models by token usage over the last month were open-weight models from China, with DeepSeek and Z.AI taking the first, second, and third spots.

OpenAI's Luna was the fourth-most-used model, up 115%.

"A model like Luna is actually about one-fifth, one-sixth the cost of, say, a Chinese open-source model," Friar told Deirdre Bosa.

"That is one of the myths of 2026 that I think we have to myth-bust," she added.

Friar explained that OpenAI saw a 10x jump in Luna usage after dropping its price by some 80% just two weeks after launching the model.

In an interview with Yahoo Finance, Santa Clara University Leavey School of Business professor Ram Bala estimated that, in the future, open-weight models will account for about 80% to 90% of total token usage, but closed models will make up the vast majority of dollars spent.

Open-weight model makers generate revenue by hosting their models on their own hardware and having customers pay to access them. Users who have access to powerful AI systems can, however, download the models for free and run them on their own.

To better compete with open models and gain an edge on their closed-weight competitors, frontier labs like OpenAI and its rivals Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Meta ( META ) have kicked off a pricing war, with each company working to improve its overall model and computing efficiency and reduce the cost to use its services for customers.

articles.title: Gen Z saving for home, Gen X for retirement
articles.summary: YouGov survey for Stable Money finds 65% of Indians start saving before 30; Gen Z saves for a home, Gen X for retirement; 80% save digitally; MFs and FDs lead.
articles.body: Chennai: Did you know that 65% of Indians, who save, begin saving or start investing well before the age of 30? 2026 has been an year of uncertainty, with the RBI projecting consumer price inflation (CPI) of 5.2% for FY27. While markets are gradually gaining stability, a latest survey by YouGov, commissioned by Stable Money in the context of the recent World Savings Day revealed how Indians save, what they save for and where they put their money into?The survey revealed, while Gen Z is saving for a home (26%), Gen X is more focused on retirement (35%). It also showed that nearly half of women savers (56%) call the shots on household money. Mutual funds and fixed deposits are neck and neck at the top: 23% pick MFs first and 21% pick bank FDs and RDs.Interestingly, between the morning commute and the evening scroll, Indians are doing what their parents once did at the bank counter: putting money away, albeit digitally - 80% of Indian savers have gone digital. “Indians always had the habit of saving. That is intact. Today it lives on the phone,” says Saurabh Jain, co-founder, Stable Money.Among women, there is a growing sense of financial independence, thanks to greater access to information via digital platforms. “Research and analysis which was earlier largely provided only by professionals such as financial advisors is now accessible at their fingertips through smartphones, further democratised by AI tools empowering women to compare financial products, assess returns and make more informed investment decisions on their own,” says Nalinakanthi V, partner, SowSampadh Partners, a Chennai-based mutual fund distributor.The report also showed that about 19% prefer fixed income to savings account, and 11% would rather reduce debt, so 87% would invest, save, or pay down debt with it. articles.title: Ramco plans construction chemicals unit at AP plant
articles.summary: Ramco Cements to invest Rs 20 crore in a 1.2 lakh-tonne construction chemicals unit at Kolimigundla, AP; targets Rs 150 crore from non-core asset sales.
articles.body: Chennai: Ramco Cements plans to invest Rs 20 crore in a new construction chemicals manufacturing unit at its Kolimigundla plant in Andhra Pradesh, even as it sticks to its Rs 800 crore capital expenditure plan for the current fiscal. The company also plans to raise about Rs 150 crore through the sale of non-core assets.The proposed unit for construction chemicals will have an annual production capacity of 1.2 lakh tonnes and is expected to be completed by the second quarter of FY28, according to the company’s investor presentation.Though Ramco has been present in the construction chemicals business for more than two decades, it has sharpened its focus on the segment in recent years, banking on its growth potential. Last year, it unveiled a new brand identity for the business, Hard Worker. The domestic construction chemicals market is projected to reach Rs 40,000 crore by 2030.The company’s construction chemicals sales volume rose to 2.04 lakh tonnes in Q2FY27 from 1.48 lakh tonnes in the year-ago period and 1.35 lakh tonnes in Q1FY27. Revenue from the business grew 31% to Rs 217 crore in the first half of FY27. Ramco has set a target of clocking revenue of Rs 2,000 crore in this business over the next four years.Ramco monetised Rs 1,098 crore through non-core asset sales in the last two years. It has identified further assets worth about Rs 150 crore for disposal in the near term, of which Rs 29 crore was realised in the first half of FY27.The company spent Rs 373 crore on capital expenditure in the first half of FY27, with its full-year capex guidance unchanged at Rs 800 crore.Ramco completed the debottlenecking of its Jayanthipuram plant in Q2 FY27, adding 0.73 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) to its capacity and taking its total cement capacity to 27.17 MTPA.The company aims to increase its cement capacity to about 31 MTPA by March 2027, with the commissioning of Line 2 at Kolimigundla. articles.title: Trump is losing his grip on the media — and other key midterm lessons
articles.summary: Last week’s midterm elections were chock full of lessons for both the right and left. And there were many takeaways about the media industry, too.
articles.body: Last week’s midterm elections were chock full of lessons for both the right and left. And there were many takeaways about the media industry, too. To name a few: The TV ad spending advantage held by Republicans wasn’t enough to hold back a “blue wave.” The pre-election Fox News ratings decline really was a foreshock, signaling that GOP voters were feeling discouraged about their party. And the election season showed that Democrats have figured out how to compete with President Donald Trump in what are sometimes dubbed the “attention wars.” Now that a week has passed, and the results have sunk in, here are some of the other findings about the political media ecosystem: Trump’s time as master media manipulator might be up Remember his made-for-TV GOP midterm convention? Probably not. It failed to move the needle. Fox even stopped carrying many of his rallies live. And his attention-grabbing stunts — like an election-eve speech at the Reflecting Pool — made him look out of touch. Now, a president who prided himself on commanding the media’s attention seems to be losing his grip on it. Right-leaning media critic Jeffrey McCall wrote in a recent op-ed, “With Trump’s influence on the wane, it’s time for a different approach to journalism, one that doesn’t put Trump at the center of every story.” Democrats learned new-media tricks Successful candidates communicated in new ways and produced lots and lots of vertical videos. Substack pointed out that “all seven Democrats who flipped Republican-held Senate seats… ran a Substack publication during the race.” Democratic strategist Joshua Karp, who advised Annie Andrews’ campaign in South Carolina, said winning campaigns understood the “information bubbles” that voters, donors and reporters inhabit. “The concept of information bubbles isn’t a particularly new one, but 2026 was a breakout cycle for campaigns that treated them seriously, from Jon Ossoff’s clipping strategy to Abdul [El-Sayed]’s choreographed TikTok dances,” he said, crediting a younger generation of candidates who are “native to the grammar of the modern information ecosystem.” Many pre-election polls were wrong “The polls were wildly inaccurate,” outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson said Monday. That’s true, insofar as many — not all — polls wildly underestimated Democrats’ leads ahead of election day. But there’s been relatively little hullabaloo since the polls were directionally correct, capturing the public mood and showing Democrats ahead. “Unpredictable electorates can lead to overcorrecting after presidential elections,” the Financial Times explained. “After a decade of underrating Donald Trump’s support, pollsters finally underestimated Democrats,” The Atlantic concluded. The approval rating polls were right “The midterms weren’t a surprise or an aberration; they were an expression of how the electorate has always felt about Trump and his movement, albeit a particularly emphatic one,” liberal columnist Paul Waldman commented Monday in Public Notice. Trump “is uniquely unpopular,” Waldman went on, and it’s worth considering whether the newsrooms that have worked hard to recognize and report on Trump’s MAGA base appeal have also worked hard enough to reflect the public’s prevailing anti-Trump sentiment. Reality reasserted itself For years, Trump’s lies “never seemed to catch up with him, no matter how much they were fact-checked,” New York Times columnist Lydia Polgreen wrote. However, “Americans know their own wallets” and “they know that, Trump’s dismissal notwithstanding, the affordability crisis is no hoax.” The Trumpian reality distortion field is long gone.” Investigative reporting had an impact Writing from Maine, media historian Michael Socolow asserted that aggressive media coverage was a key factor in Sen. Susan Collins’ loss to Troy Jackson: “Corruption was a major theme in this campaign, and its resonance with recent independent, critical and accurate reporting in the Maine media undoubtedly damaged Collins,” he wrote on his Substack. Last-minute dramas didn’t matter much at all Remember the Haley Stevens endorsement-switching fiasco that consumed insiders in the final days of the Michigan Senate race? Evidently, it didn’t matter to many voters. El-Sayed still won easily. “Recency bias is a powerful drug,” Bill Grueskin wrote for Columbia Journalism Review. “Our political press ought to read the warning label before delivering their hot takes.” The major TV networks still mattered most on election night Even in a media environment with infinite ways to watch the results, the 100-year-old NBC still attracted the most eyeballs on election night. Audiences gravitated to experts like Steve Kornacki on NBC, John King on CNN and Ali Velshi on MS NOW. According to Nielsen, more than 30 million people tuned in for prime time coverage of the midterms across about a dozen channels. Yes, audiences want to watch on their phones as well as big TVs, but they still seek out authoritative anchors even when countless other options exist. And about those… Political live streams are for super-fans Some opinionated live-streamers like Hasan Piker attracted big audiences on election night, but for the most part, live-streaming is narrow while TV is broad. “Piker drew a peak of 241,783 concurrent ⁠viewers to his election-night stream on Twitch,” according to this Reuters story. For comparison, MS NOW peaked with 4 million concurrent viewers. Now, this is not a knock on live streamers. They have a lot of influence! And they get clipped and remixed and reshared in all sorts of ways. But “views” are very different than “viewers.” Many live-streamers accumulated millions of views but only had thousands of viewers at any given moment. Here’s the key stat from YouTube’s election night report: “Globally, over 40 million viewers watched livestreams related to the U.S. midterm elections, with viewership peaking at over 3 million concurrent viewers at 10:19 p.m. ET.” At that same time, CNN averaged 4.4 million viewers, Fox News averaged 4.1 million, and so on. Trump is in a ‘digital bunker’ now And it’s called Truth Social. As New York magazine’s John Herrman wrote, the president’s retreat to his increasingly deserted social platform may preview his political future: “An endless series of posts seen by fewer and fewer people, many of whom aren’t sure why they need to listen to them anymore.”

articles.title: Credit card debt mounts amid Democrats’ push to cap interest rates
articles.summary: New data shows Americans’ credit card balances are mounting, as some Democratic lawmakers push for capping interest rates. Credit card balances increased by $22 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 1.7 percent relative to the second quarter, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported Tuesday. Credit card debt for this year topped…
articles.body:
New data shows Americans’ credit card balances are mounting, as some Democratic lawmakers push for capping interest rates.

Credit card balances increased by $22 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 1.7 percent relative to the second quarter, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported Tuesday .

Credit card debt for this year topped $1.28 trillion, as credit card balances in the third quarter were $52 billion greater than they were in the third quarter of 2025, according to the New York Fed .

Roughly 6.9 percent of credit card holders flowed into “serious delinquency” in the third quarter, meaning they missed at least three straight monthly payments. That is lower than the 7.05 percent of holders who flowed into serious delinquency in quarter three of 2025.

President Trump in January called on credit card companies to cap interest rates at 10 percent for one year. The average credit card interest rate was 19.71 percent as of Wednesday, according to Bankrate .

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said Sunday she wants to codify that cap, as Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January

“I got the bill, I’m ready to go,” Warren said on CBS News’s “ Face the Nation .” The Massachusetts Democrats is in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee.

Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) also campaigned on capping interest rates, calling credit card companies “predatory.”

But Jessica Riedl, a budget and tax fellow at the Brookings Institution who worked for former Sen. Rob Portman (R-Ohio), argued that capping interest rates will result in banks cancelling the credit cards of “everyone with a credit score under 750.”

She wrote on social platform X , “I bet they’ll love having to instead rely on payday loans, pawn shops, and local loan sharks to provide quick credit in a pinch.”

articles.title: US Push for Higher German Drug Prices Would Backfire, Study Says
articles.summary: US pressure on Germany to raise drug prices in an effort to spread the burden of research funding more equitably would ultimately backfire and cost both coun...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- US pressure on Germany to raise drug prices in an effort to spread the burden of research funding more equitably would ultimately backfire and cost both countries more, according to a new study.

The Trump administration argues that Germany has consistently been underpaying for drugs and needs to contribute more to pharmaceutical research and development. In June, it launched a tariff probe which referenced German healthcare reforms passed this year that pare back spending on medicines to relieve pressure on the federal budget.

At the same time, the US, which typically has the highest global drug prices, is seeking to reduce outlays by tying spending to a mechanism that caps it at the lowest, or near-lowest, price in a basket of countries, including Germany.

That inconsistency means the argument that higher German prices would lead to lower costs for American patients isn't supported, according to a study commissioned by Germany's GKV National Association of Statutory Health Insurance Funds published Wednesday.

Instead, if Germany were to increase drug prices by 25% — mirroring a US-UK deal last year — it would reduce net annual projected savings in Medicaid spending by about $300 million. The burden would be considerably higher for Germany, where a 25% hike would add about €5.5 billion ($6.2 billion) to outlays on drugs.

The "internal contradictions" of the two instruments the US is pursuing were part of the motivation for the study, according to author Thomas Hwang, an expert on pharmaceutical pricing and regulation.

The findings "call into question the underlying assumption that US payers would benefit from higher German prices," Hwang said in an interview. "Ultimately, the higher costs will be borne by taxpayers and patients, and it would harm both the US and Germany."

As well as the US government, the pharmaceutical industry has long been lobbying for higher drug prices in Europe, warning that failing to raise them could hold back product launches and constrain investment.

In the UK, drugmakers last year secured a reduction in the rebates they pay to the National Health Service after saying the environment there made Britain "uninvestable." As part of the deal with the US, Washington agreed not to impose tariffs on UK pharmaceutical exports for at least three years.

articles.summary: By Kanishka Singh WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Five US states have joined the Federal Trade Commission in a lawsuit that alleges telehealth company Hims &...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Five US states have joined the Federal Trade Commission in a lawsuit that ‌alleges telehealth company Hims & Hers Health engaged in deceptive ‌and unlawful privacy practices, the FTC said on Tuesday.

The lawsuit alleges the company ​shared consumers' sensitive health information with third-party advertising platforms including Meta Platforms and Snap, despite claiming its services maintain consumers' privacy.

The case also contends Hims & Hers deceives users about its billing and cancellation ‌practices, according to the ⁠FTC.

The amended complaint filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California now includes ⁠Arizona, Florida, Nebraska, Ohio and Wisconsin and alleges violations of the states' consumer protection laws in addition to federal laws, the FTC said ​in ​a statement.

Los Angeles County and Utah ​joined the action when ‌the FTC initiated it in July.

Hims & Hers is one of the largest telehealth players in the market for weight-loss drugs. It also treats erectile dysfunction, hair loss and mental health conditions, shipping prescriptions directly to customers.

"We will vigorously defend ourselves against these follow-on ‌claims, which rely on the same flawed ​allegations advanced in the government's lawsuit," ​a Hims & Hers spokesperson ​said on Tuesday.

The FTC alleged Hims & Hers charges ‌users for prescription drugs before they ​meet with healthcare ​providers and makes it difficult to cancel subscriptions.

The company cut its full-year core profit forecast on Monday as higher costs ​tied to a ‌pivot to branded weight-loss drugs and international expansion pressured ​margins.
